releases.text: Refined recommended stacks to weigh who reviews and uses each tool at that GTM team size, not only the category-wide value score. Large list building now counts Apollo Organization (25 seats, billed annually, quote needed) instead of the free Starter plan; Large enrichment moves from Hunter to Clay (Growth list price plus an Enterprise quote for SSO). Scaling list building now counts Apollo Basic for 10 seats. Added ZoomInfo as contact sales (not in any stack). Sources and G2 reviewer company-size mixes are on the Scaling and Large pages.

Recommended stacks are now organized by GTM team size (solo founder 1, small team 2–5, early scaling 6–15, scaling 16–40, large / multi-team 40+) instead of funding stage, with use cases to skip at each size. Estimated totals changed accordingly; earlier entries below refer to the old stage names. Added an Articles section. Prices were last checked 2026-11-02; vendor security statements on the large-team page were checked 2026-11-05.

Price check of all 41 tools: no change to any price used in our stage stacks (totals unchanged). Kit now shows public prices (Free up to 10,000 subscribers; Creator $33/mo billed yearly) and Apollo confirms a free Starter plan; Clay shows a free plan (500 actions/mo); Webflow's $25 CMS plan is now named Premium; Surfer lists new AI Visibility ($82/mo) and Peace of Mind ($299/mo) tiers. Prices for Woodpecker, Clearout, Canva and Discord could not be verified.

Salesforce announced Hunter, an outbound sales agent on Agentforce with ZoomInfo and Demandbase as launch data partners; Demandbase says it is in pilot with general availability planned later in 2026. Not listed or priced yet.
AnySoft announced general availability of Anya, a team sales agent configured by RevOps that drafts follow-ups and updates CRM records. Not listed or priced yet.
EvaSpeaks launched an omnichannel AI agent platform that qualifies leads from phone, website and email conversations, books appointments and updates CRM leads. Not listed or priced yet.
Price check: Instantly Outreach Hypergrowth is $97/mo (125,000 emails/mo); Light Speed is $358/mo. Our later-stage stack now uses Hypergrowth, lowering its estimate from $4,145 to $3,884/mo.

Added 7 marketing use cases (SEO & content, social scheduling, landing pages, newsletters, design & video, community, web analytics) and 18 tools; solo and pre-seed to Series A stacks now include a marketing section.
Directory launched (draft) with 23 tools across 8 use cases. Weekly release and price-change log coming.

solo.who: One person doing all of go-to-market: you are the founder, the seller and the marketer. Your goal is the first repeatable customers, not a machine.
solo.assumptions: 1 GTM person, 1 LinkedIn account, light volume. Hunter's free plan (50 credits/mo) caps how many new emails you can find; move up when you outgrow it. Monthly billing, entry tiers; Carrd is priced yearly ÷ 12.
bytool: Spreadsheet or notes app you already own. Message everyone you know who fits your ICP first; no tool is needed to do this.
Customer conversations plus a one-page doc. We list no paid tool for this job: talk to buyers first.
items: Highest value score for list building (free, fit 5/5). Exa is a free alternative if you prefer search-style prospecting. Free-plan limits change, so check them.
Free email finding and verification is enough for light hand-built lists.
Lowest published entry price for outbound email in our list. Instantly scores higher on value (94 vs 88) but costs $8 more; revisit at 2–5 people.
Cheapest listed LinkedIn tool and the best value score in its category. Per user, billed in euros.
Cheapest custom-domain landing page in our list; $19/yr is the yearly price on its Pro page.
Highest value score; free until you monetize. Kit is the free alternative (free up to 10,000 subscribers).
Free and good enough for basic traffic and source tracking at this size.
skip: Signals & intent data (RB2B, PostHog, Common Room)
Paid intent and visitor-identification tools tell you who to talk to. Until hand-built outbound gets replies, you have nobody to prioritize.
AI SDR / agentic SDR
These are contact-sales products. An agent cannot fix messaging that does not work by hand yet.
Social scheduling, SEO tooling, design/video, community
Useful later; none of them is needed to get the first customers.

small.who: Two to five people share go-to-market. Warm intros and hand outbound already produce some meetings, and you now want a repeatable sequence plus a little content.
small.assumptions: 3 GTM people, 2 LinkedIn users, ~5,000 emails/mo, monthly billing, entry tiers. Waalaxy is priced per user in euros and not converted.
bytool: Still your best channel. Keep it in a shared spreadsheet or your CRM.
Revisit with real call notes; no paid tool listed for this job.
items: Highest value score for list building; free. Check current free-plan limits.
Hunter shares one credit pool across unlimited team members (vendor help center), so adding people does not add seats.
Highest value score for outbound (94). Unlimited mailboxes on one plan; its lead credits are not added because Hunter covers enrichment.
Light LinkedIn volume at the lowest per-user price. Move to HeyReach when you run many senders.
Free first-party search data. Paid content tools wait until you publish weekly.
Free for up to 3 channels; best value score in its category (tied with Typefully).
Multi-page site with your own domain for content/SEO. Carrd is cheaper but single-page.
Free web analytics; add product/funnel analytics later.
Optional, and only if warm intros plus outbound are already booking meetings: free website-visitor identification to prioritize follow-up.
skip: Paid signals & intent data
Use at most the free RB2B plan, and only once outbound is booking meetings.
AI SDR / agentic SDR
Contact-sales pricing and little to feed it yet.
Paid SEO tools (Surfer), video, community
Use Search Console and publish first; add paid tools once content is a weekly habit.

early.who: Six to fifteen people run go-to-market: dedicated sellers, someone owning content, and enough volume that tooling gaps cost real pipeline.
early.assumptions: 10 GTM people, 5 LinkedIn senders, ~25,000 emails/mo (inside Instantly's 125,000/mo Hypergrowth tier), monthly billing. Surfer is its yearly-billed view; Framer is its yearly-billing view. PostHog counted at its free allowance (usage-based beyond it).
bytool: Track in your CRM; keep investing, it is still your cheapest channel.
Refresh quarterly from win/loss notes; no paid tool listed.
items: Free is for 'exploring or very light usage' per Apollo; we count $0 for light list pulls, but 6-15 people will likely outgrow it. Basic is $49/seat/mo billed annually (not counted). 28% of Apollo's 9,858 G2 reviewers are mid-market (51-1,000 employees).
Clearer enrichment: more credits shared across unlimited team members, and verification before sending.
Full outbound volume on one plan; highest value score for outbound.
Built for many senders (fit 5/5). Waalaxy is cheaper per seat if you only need light LinkedIn volume.
Signals become useful at this volume: identifies site visitors to feed outbound.
Free first-party data on which queries bring visitors.
Content as a system: optimization is a separate job from tracking. Discovery is its lowest listed tier.
Team scheduling beyond Buffer’s free 3-channel limit.
Design-led site with custom domain; lowest paid tier.
Free until you monetize (Lite is $49/mo, yearly-billing view).
Real product and funnel analytics (a separate job from visitor identification); usage-based beyond the free allowance.
skip: AI SDR / agentic SDR
Optional and contact-sales. Hire or train humans first; add an agent only when the motion is proven and measured.
Paid intent platforms (Common Room)
$2,500/mo billed annually is poor value until you have enough volume for multi-channel intent to change who you call.
Community, video
Only if a specific channel is already working.

scaling.who: Sixteen to forty people in go-to-market, several managers, and RevOps starting to own reports, permissions and data hygiene.
scaling.assumptions: 25 GTM people, 10 LinkedIn senders, high email volume (125,000/mo), monthly list prices except Apollo (10 prospecting seats, billed annually); Webflow and Surfer are yearly-billed views. RB2B Pro is a 'from' price. PostHog counted at its free allowance (usage-based beyond it).
bytool: Sourced and tracked in the CRM, not a tool in this stack.
Owned by product marketing; no paid tool listed.
items: Free is for 'exploring or very light usage' per Apollo, so we count Basic for the 10 people who prospect ($49/seat/mo billed annually, credits pooled across the team). 28% of Apollo's 9,858 G2 reviewers are mid-market (51-1,000 employees), roughly 2,800 reviewers. Professional ($79) adds waterfall enrichment, which overlaps Hunter, so it is not counted. Confirm seats and credits with the vendor.

Largest listed tier; unlimited team members share one credit pool, so no per-seat cost. G2 shows 31.9% of Hunter's 659 reviewers are mid-market (about 210) versus 24.8% of Clay's 234 (about 58), so Clay is not clearly the mid-market pick. Step up to Clay Growth ($495/mo monthly list) when RevOps needs CRM auto-sync, phone numbers and signals; the Large stack uses Clay.
Cost-first pick at this volume. Test its admin and role controls in the trial; Reply.io is the step-up when you need org-level roles (see Large).
Multi-seat: its help center documents Admin and Member roles with per-feature permissions.
Signals are core at this size. RB2B Pro is the lowest-cost listed paid tier; Common Room ($2,500/mo) is the step-up for community and multi-channel signals.
Content optimization, a separate job from tracking.
Social scheduling across a marketing team.
CMS-capable site for a content team; lowest CMS tier on its pricing page.
Free until you monetize; Pro is $95/mo (yearly-billing view).
Queryable product/funnel analytics. Pipeline and revenue reporting belong in your CRM, which this directory does not cover.
skip: AI SDR / agentic SDR
Still optional. Run a measured pilot against human outbound; do not replace the team on a demo.
Common Room
Wait until RB2B-level signals are clearly insufficient.
Video and community tools
Optional, not counted.
evidence: Pricing page (checked 2026-11-05): Basic $49, Professional $79 per seat/mo billed annually. G2: of 9,858 reviews, 28.4% mid-market (51-1,000 employees) and 4.6% enterprise, so most reviewers are smaller teams but the mid-market base is large.

G2 comparison (checked 2026-11-05): Hunter has 659 reviews (31.9% mid-market); Clay has 234 (24.8% mid-market, 1.4% enterprise). Clay's reviewers cite a learning curve and credit use. Neither review base is clearly mid-market-led, so we keep the cheaper pick here.
scaling.evidence_title: What we found: who reviews our list-building and enrichment picks

large.who: More than forty people across several teams or regions. Procurement, security review and data-processing agreements are part of buying anything.
large.assumptions: 40+ GTM people across teams, 25 of them prospecting in Apollo (Organization, billed annually, 3-seat minimum), ~25 LinkedIn senders (HeyReach Agency tier), monthly list prices except Apollo and Common Room (billed annually, Common Room 5 seats). Clay is its Growth monthly list price; its Enterprise tier is custom. Reply.io is a 'from' price: its higher tiers vary and need a quote. Enterprise tiers, SSO and security documents are quote-based. This total is a floor, not a quote.
bytool: Owned by product marketing; no paid tool listed.
items: Not the free Starter: 40+ people need SSO and admin controls, which Apollo sells on Organization ($119/seat/mo billed annually) and its Custom plan. Size evidence: of 9,858 G2 reviews, 28% come from mid-market and 5% from enterprise companies (roughly 2,800 and 450 reviewers), Apollo publishes a 130-rep customer story (Superside), and it lists SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 in its trust center. Seats assumed: 25 of your 40+ people prospect. ZoomInfo has a larger enterprise review share (26%) but no public price: quote both.

Clay's Enterprise tier lists SSO/SAML, SCIM, role-based access, IP allowlists and a custom DPA, it states SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, and its case studies include Intercom, Verkada and Rippling. Hunter's public pages list a custom enterprise volume plan but no SSO. Caveat: Clay's G2 reviewers skew small (74% under 51 employees, 1% enterprise), with a learning curve and fast credit use as top complaints, so pilot with credit budgets. $495 is Growth's monthly list price; SSO and RBAC need the Enterprise quote.

Documents organization, multi-team and single-team roles and permissions in its help center, and says it is SOC 2 certified. Pricing beyond the entry tier needs a quote. Instantly ($97 at 125,000 emails/mo) is cheaper if your security team accepts its attestation.
$999/mo for 25 senders beats $79 × 25. Roles are documented, but we found no SOC 2 claim and its DPA says SSO is not currently supported: confirm with security.
Vendor security page lists a SOC 2 Type 2 report, GDPR and CCPA, SSO/SAML/SCIM and role-based access.
Content optimization; check seat limits for multiple teams.
CMS-capable site; lowest CMS tier. Enterprise plans are quote-based.
Product/funnel analytics, usage-based beyond the free allowance.
Only after a measured pilot: contact sales is fine at this size when the need is real. 11x and Qualified are the other listed options.
skip: Newsletter tooling
Brand and lifecycle email usually sit with a marketing platform you already own; not counted.
Community and video tools
Optional, not counted.
evidence: Pricing page: Organization is $119 per seat per month billed annually with a 3-seat minimum, and SSO appears in its plan table (checked 2026-11-05). Trust center lists SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, GDPR and CCPA. Help center has an article on setting up SSO. Vendor enterprise page cites RBAC, permission profiles and audit logging; vendor customer story: Superside runs 130 reps on Apollo. These are vendor statements.

G2 comparison page (checked 2026-11-05): of 9,858 Apollo reviews, 67.0% small-business (50 or fewer employees), 28.4% mid-market (51-1,000) and 4.6% enterprise (over 1,000). That is roughly 2,800 mid-market and 450 enterprise reviewers (our arithmetic from G2's percentages).
ZoomInfo (not in our stack: contact sales)

G2 reviewers (8,728 reviews, checked 2026-11-05) are 25.8% small-business, 48.1% mid-market and 26.1% enterprise, the most enterprise-heavy list-building voice we found. It publishes no price (priced by licenses and credits). Vendor security materials state SOC 2 Type II and ISO certifications. Request a quote next to Apollo's.

Vendor pricing page (checked 2026-11-05): states SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR and CCPA. Enterprise (custom pricing, annual commitment) adds SSO/SAML, SCIM, RBAC, user groups with credit budgets, IP allowlists, and a custom CSA and DPA; Launch and Growth do not include SSO or RBAC. Named customer case studies on the page include Intercom, Verkada, Rippling and Hex. Growth is $495/mo monthly list ($446 annual view). G2: 234 reviews, 73.8% small-business, 24.8% mid-market, 1.4% enterprise; Hunter (659 reviews) shows 31.9% mid-market.

G2 reviewer mix for our Large outbound pick: Reply.io is 80.5% small-business, 17.4% mid-market, 2.1% enterprise (1,568 reviews). HeyReach has only 74 G2 reviews. No tool we list for these jobs has a large mid-market or enterprise review base; Outreach (59.2% mid-market, 21.7% enterprise) and Salesloft (50.9%, 32.6%) do, but they are not listed. We did not change these picks and flag the gap.
Vendor security page lists a SOC 2 Type 2 report, GDPR and CCPA compliance, SSO/SAML/SCIM and role-based access control.
Help center documents organization, multi-team and single-team roles and permissions; vendor white-label page says the platform is SOC 2 certified.
Help center documents Admin and Member roles with per-feature permissions. Its data processing addendum says SSO (including SAML) is not currently supported, and we found no SOC 2 claim.
Help center: unlimited team members at no extra cost on one shared credit pool, with Owner, Admin and Member roles. Vendor says a DPA is included and SOC 2 is for enterprise.
Public sources we found disagree on whether a SOC 2 Type II report is held. Ask the vendor for its current report under NDA before buying.
